extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing endings to novels/long-form fiction that resolve storylines and leave the reader with an intended emotional impression, while accounting for genre and market expectations. Focuses on structure (denouement), emotional tone, loose threads, and sequel/series considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include the denouement
rubrics_metrics.description: The resolution of the story (denouement) should follow from the climax and allow time for the dust of the climax to settle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t end immediately at the climax; avoid manuscripts that have only a couple pages after the climax. The denouement should flow naturally from the turning point and fully resolve the conflict without dragging on for excessive pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve the central conflict fully
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the protagonist’s main conflict is properly resolved in a way that follows logically from the climax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers expect the main plotline to reach a clear resolution in the ending; resolving the protagonist’s arc neatly is essential to reader satisfaction. Avoid leaving the primary conflict ambiguous unless purposefully chosen for thematic reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tie up (or intentionally leave) loose ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Check and follow through on all dangling plot threads—subplots, secondary characters, and outstanding decisions—unless you intentionally leave them unresolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers sometimes focus on the protagonist and forget other threads (e.g., a sibling’s marital decision). Use outlining (before or after drafting) to track threads. If you leave threads 'untied' do so deliberately and consistently with the story's aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide and deliver the intended reader feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Before finishing, consider what emotion you want the reader to feel when they close the book (e.g., overjoyed, content, peaceful, energized, heartbroken).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose an emotional target and shape the ending to produce it. Avoid ending with feelings of confusion or disappointment. Match the ending’s emotional pitch to the story—don’t abruptly swing from a dark climax to an ecstatic resolution unless it makes narrative sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure emotional truth and consistency (endings must ring true)
rubrics_metrics.description: An ending should feel authentic to the characters and the overall mood of the work, even if it is not conventionally happy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use character motivation and established tone to justify the ending. The post quotes The Sun Also Rises as an example of a poignant, bittersweet ending that 'rings true' to characters and mood despite not being happy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know genre requirements (happy endings when required)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some genres demand a happy or optimistic ending (e.g., romance usually requires an 'emotionally satisfying and optimistic ending' — HEA or HFN).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of conventions and formal expectations (Romance Writers of America guidance cited). If writing within a genre that expects an optimistic ending, plan your resolution accordingly to meet reader/publisher expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider marketplace and commercial vs. literary expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial novels tend to have happier, more satisfying endings; literary novels commonly allow more ambiguity and less tidy resolutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing your ending, consider where the book sits in the market. Even if not a strict genre rule, commercial viability and reader expectations vary by category and should influence tonal and plot choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid gratuitous cliffhangers (make books satisfy on their own)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not end the book on a major unresolved peril simply to force a sequel; most books should be satisfying as standalones, even if they leave room for continuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Debut writers sometimes rely on a cliffhanger to attempt to build a series, but publishers may only buy one book. Safer to craft an ending that stands on its own while leaving optional threads for sequels. Example: Holly Black’s approach of ending with the protagonist in a safe spot—a natural pause rather than a perilous cliffhanger—is recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance series continuity with standalone satisfaction
rubrics_metrics.description: If you plan a series, leave room for future development but provide a satisfying conclusion to the book’s particular narrative arc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Endings can be a 'natural pause' that resolves the immediate vein of conflict while keeping larger arcs open; this keeps readers satisfied and publishers comfortable buying individual volumes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use outlining and revision tools to track ending needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ outlining (before or after drafting) to ensure you’ve accounted for denouement, plot threads, and emotional beats needed in the ending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outlining helps prevent tunnel vision on the protagonist’s main arc and assists in identifying unresolved subplots or emotional mismatches between climax and resolution.
